name: LinkedIn style: the feed's retry death spiral (2018 load test)
description: Opening the home feed: client → API front door (Voyager-API) → Feed Mixer (ranking, blending) → FollowFeed broker → D2 (client-side load balancing) → FollowFeed storage nodes (4 replicas of one partition, about 1,200 QPS each, with an in-node read-through cache and the data in RocksDB). The Mixer also hydrates (Espresso + cache) and reads ranking features (Venice). Posting goes Kafka → Partitioner → index writes. In a load test in 2018-02, memory ran short on one storage host and its latency soared; the broker timed out after 400 ms and sent to another replica after 150 ms, and the other 3 replicas overloaded too; Jetty's queue limit of 5,000 let requests wait until they had long timed out and still be done (wasted work). The fix: a queue limit of 500, timeouts aligned at 400 ms, retry limits per host (about 2.5% of the peak), and servers answering 429. Sources: https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/optimization/making-linkedin-s-organic-feed-handle-peak-traffic , https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/feed/followfeed-linkedin-s-feed-made-faster-and-smarter . Only the replica set of one partition is drawn; the fan-out to the other partitions is not.

notes.text: Try this: 1) Run the scenario: in seconds 20–50 a load test pushes traffic to 1.25 times, and storage node #0 becomes 10 times slower (memory pressure, constant GC). The other 3 cannot take its load, retries on d2→storage add more, and a queue limit of 5,000 lets requests wait until they have timed out and still be done (about 52% fail here, p99 about 2 seconds). The spike alone, or one slow node alone, causes no trouble. 2) Set the storage nodes' queue limit to 500 (LinkedIn's fix): about 27% fail. 3) Also give d2→storage a retry budget of 0.025 (about 2.5% of the peak): about 16% fail, p99 down to about 630 ms. 4) Turn on deadline propagation for the members, or outlier ejection on D2, and compare.

Simplified: a real broker fans out to many partitions at once and merges all the results, so the slowest partition sets the latency. A service in the simulator calls each downstream, but one kind of downstream has one connection, so only the replica set of one partition is drawn. Jetty has two queues (accept and request); here they are one queue limit.
